title: Other ways of adding information to noun phrases 1: additional noun phrases, etc.
subtitle: Dr Alex Parr, director of the State Museum
summary: Add information to a noun phrase with a second noun phrase, with namely or that is, and with participle and to-infinitive clauses.

lesson.heading: Two noun phrases, one person or thing
lesson.text: We often add information about a person or thing by talking about the same person or thing again in a following noun phrase. In writing the two items are usually separated by a comma, and in speech by a pause or another intonation break.

examples.text: A hooded cobra, **one of the world's most dangerous snakes**, has escaped from Dudley Zoo.
Dr Alex Parr, **director of the State Museum**, is to become the government's arts adviser.
Four kilos of Beluga caviar, **among the most expensive foods in the world**, has been ordered for the reception.

left.label: With commas - extra information
left.text: The second phrase simply adds a detail, like a non-defining relative clause.
examples: Dr Sofia Lopez, **head of Downlands Hospital**, has criticised government plans to cut health funding.

right.label: No comma - it says which one
right.text: When the second item works like a defining relative clause - usually a name - there is no punctuation and no intonation break.
examples: My friend **Mia** has moved to Sweden.
The current champion is expected to survive her first-round match with the Italian **Silvia Farina**.
One of the most popular modern writers for children is the Australian **John Marsden**.

lesson.heading: Joining with and or or
lesson.text: A conjunction can link the two noun phrases. With and the second phrase adds another role the same person has; with or it gives another name for the same thing.

examples.text: Kurt Svensson, her teacher **and** well-known concert pianist, thinks that she has great talent.
examples.note: = her teacher is also a well-known concert pianist

examples.text: Phonetics **or** the study of speech sounds is a common component on courses in teaching English as a foreign language.
Tonya's father, **and** (her) trainer for the last ten years, was in the crowd to watch her victory.

lesson.heading: namely and that is
lesson.text: The adverb namely and the phrase that is introduce the specific details behind a general noun phrase.

examples.text: This side effect of the treatment, **namely** weight gain, is counteracted with other drugs.
The main cause of global warming, **that is** the burning of fossil fuels, is to be the focus of negotiations at the international conference.

lesson.heading: Participle clauses = defining relative clauses
rows: The people **living** next door come from Italy.
The people who are living next door ...
The weapon **used** in the murder has now been found.
The prisoners **being released** are all women.
The prisoners who are being released ...

lesson.heading: to-infinitive clauses
lesson.text: A to-infinitive clause can also add information to a noun phrase, often saying what the noun is for or what it consists of.

examples.text: Have you brought a book **to read**?
My decision **to resign from the company** was made after a great deal of thought.
I thought that the management's offer, **to increase staff holidays**, was a good one.

lesson.heading: Newspaper style: -ing and -ed between commas or dashes
lesson.text: In written English, particularly in newspapers, -ing and -ed clauses are also used instead of non-defining relative clauses. They are written between commas or dashes.

examples.text: The men, **wearing anoraks and hats**, made off in a stolen Volvo estate.
The proposals - **expected to be agreed by ministers** - are less radical than many employers had feared.

lesson.text: To pick the participle, turn the phrase back into a relative clause: if the verb would be active, use -ing; if it would be passive, use -ed or being + -ed.

exercises.prompt: There is a sign on the gate ___ 'Entry forbidden'.
exercises.explanation: = which says. An active relative clause becomes an -ing participle clause.

exercises.prompt: Rivers ___ into the Baltic Sea are much cleaner now than ten years ago.
exercises.explanation: = which flow into the Baltic Sea - an active verb, so -ing.

exercises.prompt: Anyone ___ further information can see me in my office.
I went to a reunion for students ___ in the physics department during the 1990s.
exercises.explanation: = who were educated - a passive verb, so the -ed participle.

exercises.prompt: The booklets ___ as we speak will be on sale later this afternoon.
exercises.explanation: = which are being printed. A present passive needs being + -ed.

exercises.prompt: Does the participle clause stand for an active or a passive relative clause?

items.text: The people living next door come from Italy.
The weapon used in the murder has now been found.
The prisoners being released are all women.
Rivers flowing into the Baltic Sea are much cleaner now.
Anyone needing further information can see me in my office.
Across the river were some of the deer introduced into the park in the 19th century.

exercises.prompt: The weapon ___ in the murder has now been found.
exercises.explanation: The weapon was used, so the clause is passive and complete: the -ed participle.

exercises.prompt: Match each beginning with its ending. Each one adds the specific detail after namely or that is.

pairs.left: Leo Tolstoy's most celebrated novel, namely War and Peace,
The two countries having land borders with the USA, namely Mexico and Canada,
pairs.right: have complained to the President about the new customs regulations.

pairs.left: The three most popular pets in Britain, namely cats, dogs and rabbits,
The capital of Estonia, that is Tallinn,
pairs.right: is situated on the Gulf of Finland.

pairs.left: The largest island in the world, that is Greenland,
The 'consumers' of education, that is students,
pairs.right: should have ways of complaining about poor teaching.

exercises.statement: The men, wearing anoraks and hats, made off in a stolen Volvo estate.
exercises.explanation: Correct. In written English an -ing clause between commas replaces a non-defining relative clause (the men, who were wearing ...).

exercises.statement: My friend, Mia, has moved to Sweden.
exercises.explanation: My friend Mia has moved to Sweden. When the second item says which person we mean - usually a name - we use no commas.

exercises.prompt: Add 'Sofia Lopez is head of Downlands Hospital' to the news sentence as a second noun phrase.
exercises.answer: Dr Sofia Lopez, head of Downlands Hospital, has criticised government plans to cut health funding.
exercises.explanation: The extra noun phrase goes between commas straight after the name.

exercises.prompt: Add the other name for rubella (German measles) to the sentence.
exercises.answer: Rubella, or German measles, is still a common childhood disease in many countries.
exercises.explanation: or introduces another name for the same thing.
